questions.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum can lead to thiamine deficiency and Wernicke’s encephalopathy, characterized by confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.

questions.question_text: A consultant psychiatrist who is lecturing a group of medical students was explaining the concept of a delusional disorder. Which one of the following is not commonly associated or descriptive of a delusional disorder?

options.text: False belief based on incorrect inference about external reality
Firmly sustained despite the beliefs of the normal population
Firmly sustained despite there being no obvious proof or evidence against
Belief system not accepted by members of one’s culture

questions.explanation: Delusional disorders typically involve non-bizarre delusions; bizarre delusions are more characteristic of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman presents with bulimia nervosa. Her height and weight are 160 cm and 60 kg, respectively. What is her body mass index (BMI)?
questions.explanation: BMI = 60 ÷ (1.60)^2 ≈ 23.44, which is more than 23.

questions.question_text: There are several conditions that need to be met in order to reduce prejudice. Which one of the following is not one of those conditions?

options.text: Interactions with a member of the out-group

correct_answer.text: Interactions with a member of the out-group

correct_answers.text: Interactions with a member of the out-group

questions.explanation: Interacting with just one member of an out-group typically does not reduce prejudice because the individual may be seen as an exception to the stereotype.

questions.question_text: The following are criteria for a valid consent, except

options.text: No misrepresentation of beneficial effects of a proposed treatment
No inclusion of information which is irrelevant to a proposed treatment

questions.explanation: Implicit consent is a recognized form of consent; valid consent requires absence of misrepresentation, coercion and irrelevant information.

questions.question_text: You are able to assess a 20-year-old man who is aggressive and angry towards the staff at the Accident and Emergency Department. Which of the following measures is least useful?

options.text: Admit own feelings and inform the patient that the staff are frightened of his aggression and anger.
Encourage the patient to verbalize his aggression and anger.
Inform the patient that restraint or seclusion will be used if necessary.
Inform the patient that physical violence is not acceptable in the hospital setting.
Offer the option of using psychotropic medication to calm the patient.

correct_answer.text: Admit own feelings and inform the patient that the staff are frightened of his aggression and anger.

correct_answers.text: Admit own feelings and inform the patient that the staff are frightened of his aggression and anger.

questions.explanation: Admitting the staff’s fear may confuse the patient and be counterproductive; clear limits and de-escalation techniques are more helpful.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with asymptomatic unequal pupils. During physical examination, her right eye shows pupillary dilatation with poor constriction to light and accommodation. Examination of lower limbs shows depressed deep tendon reflexes. The patient is most likely suffering from?
questions.explanation: Holmes–Adie syndrome presents with tonic pupils (poor light reaction and accommodation) and absent deep tendon reflexes often in young women.

questions.question_text: When interviewing a psychotic patient, it is essential to evaluate for delusions, hallucinations and, most importantly, passivity experiences. Passivity experiences, based on your understanding, include all the following, except
questions.explanation: Passivity experiences include thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, made feelings, actions, impulses and somatic passivity; thought block is not classically listed under first-rank symptoms.

questions.question_text: This is one form of suicide that has been previously proposed by Durkheim, in which the individual commits suicide due to feelings of being increasingly distanced from societal norms.
questions.explanation: Egoistic suicide occurs when individuals feel disconnected from societal norms and lack integration.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about mental state examination is correct?

options.text: During the mental state examination, a psychiatrist should ask a large range of psychopathologies to cover every diagnostic possibility.
During mental state examination, probe questions about psychopathology are best framed with technical questions.
Mental state examination is best conducted as formal exercise which follows a schema.
Serial mental state interrogations are extremely reliable methods of judging the progress of treatment or changes in a patient’s mental health.
The best clinical approach to mental state examination is in a conversational and informal manner.

correct_answer.text: The best clinical approach to mental state examination is in a conversational and informal manner.

correct_answers.text: The best clinical approach to mental state examination is in a conversational and informal manner.

questions.explanation: An informal, conversational approach encourages patients to share their experience; rigid schemas or technical jargon can inhibit rapport.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old schizophrenia patient was admitted to the psychiatric ward under the Mental Health Act. He has not been compliant with oral antipsychotics, and you have proposed depot antipsychotics to prevent relapse since he has not been compliant to the oral medication. He strongly refuses depot injection because he is scared of pain. He does not have psychotic features and understands the risks and benefits associated with depot antipsychotics. Which of the following decisions is the best option based on ethical principles?

options.text: The doctor should inject him with depot antipsychotics under the Common Law.
The doctor should inject him with depot antipsychotics because he was admitted under the Mental Health Act.
The doctor should inject him with depot antipsychotics based on his best interests.
The doctor should postpone the decision to inject him and consult the guardian board.
The doctor should not inject him with depot antipsychotics and respect his wish.

correct_answer.text: The doctor should not inject him with depot antipsychotics and respect his wish.

correct_answers.text: The doctor should not inject him with depot antipsychotics and respect his wish.

questions.explanation: Respect for autonomy requires honoring his informed refusal; without capacity impairment or acute risk, he should not be forced.

questions.question_text: According to Durkheim, anomie refers to the social disconnectedness of lack of social norms. All of the following are causes of acute anomie, except
questions.explanation: Homelessness is associated with chronic anomie; acute anomie arises from sudden life changes like migration, bereavement, redundancy or other losses.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to be found in patients with carotid artery stenosis?
questions.explanation: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) is a classic TIA symptom in carotid stenosis.

questions.question_text: The terminology ‘institutional neurosis’ was previously coined by which one of the following individuals?
questions.explanation: Barton (1959) described ‘institutional neurosis’ in patients showing apathy, withdrawal and low self-esteem in long-term institutions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is one of the first SSRIs that was introduced?
questions.explanation: Zimeldine was one of the earliest SSRIs introduced; it was later withdrawn due to adverse effects.

questions.question_text: The following are possible explanations as to why certain psychiatric disorders are more prevalent in each of the social classes, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Breeder’s hypothesis is not a recognized theory for social class differences in psychiatric disorder prevalence.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man with schizophrenia hears his thoughts being spoken aloud whenever he hears the sound of a train whistle. This psychopathological phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: A functional hallucination occurs when a real external stimulus (train whistle) triggers a simultaneous hallucination in the same sensory modality.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old expectant father experiences somatic symptoms when his wife is 3-months pregnant. He complains of morning nausea, decreased appetite, weight gain, constipation and labour pain. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: Couvade syndrome involves psychosomatic symptoms in expectant fathers during their partner’s pregnancy.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old female just went for an interview, hoping to get into Psychiatry as a core trainee. Months later, she was informed that she did not get the position and she believes that it must be because she did not perform well enough during the interview. What kind of attribution is she making?
questions.explanation: Internal attribution is assigning the cause of an event (interview outcome) to personal factors rather than external ones.

questions.question_text: A medical student wonders what terminology would be more consistent with the following definition ‘A set of beliefs about an individual, which is based on prior achievements and other social interactions, and this set of beliefs would interact and influence one’s own behaviour’. Which terminology would fit the aforementioned description?
questions.explanation: Self-image refers to a set of beliefs about oneself based on prior achievements and interactions, which influences behaviour.

questions.question_text: This is a form of memory that involves confabulation and reports of false events. Which one of the following terms best describes this form of memory?
questions.explanation: False memory involves confabulation and reports of events that did not occur.

questions.question_text: Which of the following electroencephalogram (EEG) waveforms typically has a frequency between 4 and 7.5 Hz?
questions.explanation: Theta waves have a frequency of 4–7.5 Hz and are associated with drowsiness or early sleep stages.

questions.question_text: Two main types of conformity, informational social influence and normative social influence, have been proposed. Based on Asch’s conformity theory, normative social conformity would most likely be influenced by

options.text: Highly intelligent and socially expressive individuals

questions.explanation: Normative social influence occurs when individuals conform to avoid social rejection.

questions.question_text: Cognitive dissonance theory comprises all of the following, except
questions.explanation: Selective retention is not typically listed among the core elements (selective exposure, selective attention and selective perception) used to reduce cognitive dissonance.

questions.question_text: You have been asked to review a 50-year-old man in your dementia clinic for memory problems. Apart from the memory difficulties, the caregivers also vocalized that the patient had been having other difficulties, characterized as abnormal behaviours and movement. Of importance, they shared that one of their close relatives did suffer from a similar movement disorder and passed away at a very young age. It is likely that the patient you are currently assessing has
questions.explanation: A family history of early movement disorder and dementia suggests Huntington’s disease, an autosomal dominant condition with chorea and cognitive decline.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is referred by her GP to you for experiencing multiple episodes of unusual experiences at night. She recalls that a sudden loud sound startled her in the middle of the night. Every movement became impossible and she could not speak. She had breathing difficulty and felt her body vibrating. She saw demons staring at her from the ceiling and hands appearing from the wall to strangle her. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: Sleep paralysis involves waking with inability to move or speak, often with hypnopompic hallucinations and sense of threat.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman reports that other patients’ heads appear to be enlarged as compared to their actual body size. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: Dysmegalopsia (Alice in Wonderland syndrome) involves apparent changes in size (macropsia or micropsia).

questions.question_text: You are about to conduct an animal study. The suppliers of animals have a group of mice with reduced expression of glucocorticoid receptors and behavioural problems. Which of the following psychiatric disorders in humans would this group of mice closely resemble?
questions.explanation: Reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression is implicated in the pathophysiology of depression.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman suffers from a severe depressive episode. She has three young children studying in a primary school. She is unemployed with no coding relationship. Which of the following works provides an explanation in her case?

options.text: Brown and Harris: Social Origins of Depression
Habermas J: The Theory of Communicative Action
Sullivan HS: The Interpersonal Theory of Psychiatry

correct_answer.text: Brown and Harris: Social Origins of Depression

correct_answers.text: Brown and Harris: Social Origins of Depression

questions.explanation: Brown and Harris studied how social factors like unemployment and childcare stress contribute to depression.

questions.question_text: The following are protective factors against depressive disorder in men, except
questions.explanation: Excessive social support can reduce personal control and may contribute to depression.

questions.question_text: The early psychosis intervention team wants to develop a new community support programme to reduce the suicide risk amongst people with schizophrenia. Which of the following groups of patients is the most at risk of suicide?

options.text: Schizophrenia patients who have never been admitted in the past

questions.explanation: Nonpsychotic or high-functioning patients with schizophrenia and good insight face higher suicide risk.

questions.question_text: There is evidence that media reports of suicide can be associated with further suicides. The editor of a local newspaper would like to consult you on the appropriate way to report suicide. You would recommend all of the following, except

options.text: Encourage distressed people to seek help after reading the article
Reporting followed by advertisements for helplines

questions.explanation: Suppression of suicide reporting is not advised; responsible, factual reporting with supportive resources is recommended.

questions.question_text: This particular form of memory comprises largely procedural knowledge.
questions.explanation: Implicit memory (procedural learning) is recalled automatically and involves skills and conditioned responses.

questions.question_text: Classical and operant learning involve this particular type of memory.
questions.explanation: Both classical and operant conditioning involve implicit memory systems that support learning without conscious recall.

questions.question_text: This form of memory involves both the visual association cortex and the auditory association cortex.
questions.explanation: Sensory memory has components like iconic (visual) and echoic (auditory) memory, relying on respective association cortices.

questions.question_text: This form of memory involves both the temporal lobe and the occipital area.
questions.explanation: Verbal short-term memory involves the left temporo-occipital region; nonverbal spans involve right-sided areas.

questions.question_text: This particular form of memory requires a deliberate act of recollection and can be reported verbally.
questions.explanation: Explicit memory (also declarative memory) requires conscious retrieval and can be described in words.

questions.question_text: This refers to the memory loss from the time of the accident to the time that the patient can give a clear account of recent events.
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic amnesia is the inability to form new memories from the time of injury until recovery.

questions.question_text: This particular form of amnesia is usually associated with indifference.
questions.explanation: Psychogenic amnesia features sudden memory loss with a lack of concern (la belle indifférence) and often follows stress.

questions.question_text: This refers to the loss of memory for events that occurred prior to an event or condition.
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is difficulty recalling events that took place before the onset of amnesia.

questions.question_text: This particular form of memory is associated with confabulation, report of false events and false confessions.
questions.explanation: False memory syndrome involves detailed but inaccurate recollections, often with confabulation.

questions.question_text: This particular form of memory loss is associated with abrupt onset of disorientation, loss of ability to encode recent memories and retrograde amnesia for variable duration.
questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia presents with sudden anterograde amnesia, some retrograde loss and preserved alertness, resolving in hours.

questions.question_text: John came into the emergency department demanding to see the nurse who treated him 2 weeks ago. He claimed that she was in love with him.
questions.explanation: Erotomania (De Clérambault’s syndrome) is the delusional belief that another person, often of higher status, is in love with the patient.

questions.question_text: Ross was sent into the emergency services following an attempt to burn herself in the backyard of her garden. She tells the doctors that she is dead and her intestines are rotting.
questions.explanation: Nihilistic delusion involves belief in personal nonexistence or bodily destruction, as in Cotard’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: Peter has been feeling that a double of himself exists somewhere.
questions.explanation: Doppelganger (subjective double) is the delusional belief that a double of oneself exists.

questions.question_text: Mary has been avoiding picking up the phone calls and watching the television. She claims that the people on the television are speaking about her.
questions.explanation: Delusion of reference is the belief that neutral events (TV comments) are directed at oneself.

questions.question_text: A core trainee was asked to see Samuel who strongly believes that he is pregnant. He has been feeling this way since he learned of the news that his wife was pregnant 6 months ago.
questions.explanation: Delusion of pregnancy is a fixed belief of being pregnant despite contrary evidence.

questions.question_text: Gillian has been to multiple dermatologists seeking help as she believes that she needs treatment for her skin condition. She believes that her skin is infested by parasites.
questions.explanation: Delusion of infestation (Ekbom’s syndrome) is the false belief of being infested with parasites.

questions.question_text: The high risk factors for this condition are aggressiveness and impulsivity. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for suicide in personality disorder include mood lability, aggressiveness, impulsivity, social isolation and comorbid substance misuse.

questions.question_text: There is an estimated 15% mortality from suicide in this condition. Usually it tends to occur later in the course of the illness and especially in those who are depressed.
questions.explanation: Alcoholism carries about a 15% suicide mortality, often later in illness and associated with depression.

questions.question_text: In this condition, nearly 90% of the patients have a history of para-suicide and with a high proportion having threatened suicide in the preceding month.
questions.explanation: Neurotic disorders show about 90% history of para-suicide and frequent recent threats.

questions.question_text: In this condition, there is 15% mortality from suicide. Men who are older, separated, widowed, living alone and not working are predisposed. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Affective psychosis (mood disorder) shows about 15% suicide mortality, especially in depressed phases and older men.

questions.question_text: In this condition, there is 10% mortality from suicide. Those who commit suicide are usually young, male and unemployed and usually with chronic relapsing illness.
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia has about 10% suicide mortality, typically young males with chronic relapsing course.

questions.question_text: It is advisable to have close monitoring of patients post discharge.
questions.explanation: Primary prevention aims to reduce incidence; close post‐discharge monitoring can prevent new episodes and self-harm.

questions.question_text: It is advised that people with a strong family history of depression should space out their pregnancies to prevent poor parenting of the child.
questions.explanation: Primary prevention addresses risk factors to reduce new cases; spacing pregnancies may reduce stress and onset.

questions.question_text: This refers to the early detection and treatment of psychiatric conditions.
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early identification and intervention to halt progression.

questions.question_text: It is recommended that there is better community support and enhanced psychiatric outreach efforts. Which form of prevention is this?
questions.explanation: Tertiary prevention aims to reduce disability and improve quality of life in established illness through community support.

questions.question_text: The staff of a hostel for learning disability patients want to train their clients to clean up the tables after meals. They develop a successive reinforcing schedule to reward their clients. The clients will be rewarded successively over time for removing their utensils from the dining table into the kitchen. Then they need to wash and dry the utensils and put them back into the right drawers. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Shaping involves successive approximation, reinforcing each step toward the final behaviour.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old son of a woman is scared of dogs. His mother tries to reduce his fear by bringing him to see the dogs in the park. The fear-provoking situation is coupled and opposed by putting him on her lap and allowing him to drink his favourite juice. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition pairs the feared stimulus with a positive response to inhibit fear.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman staying in London develops fear of the tube (underground metro) and she sees a psychologist for psychotherapy. The psychologist has drafted a behavioural programme in which the patient is advised to start with travelling between two tube stations with her husband and gradually increase this to more stations without her husband. At the end of the hierarchy, she will travel alone on the long journey from Heathrow terminal station to Cockfosters station along almost the entire length of the Piccadilly line. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization uses a fear hierarchy and relaxation to reduce phobic anxiety.

questions.question_text: Aripiprazole (Choose three options.)
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is a 5-HT1A partial agonist, a 5-HT2A antagonist and a D2 partial agonist.

questions.question_text: Diazepam (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Diazepam is a GABA-A agonist.

questions.question_text: Lofexidine (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Lofexidine is an alpha2 agonist.

questions.question_text: His psychotic symptoms are not controlled. His mother wants to know the minimum effective dose (in mg) of risperidone in his case. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: The minimum effective dose of risperidone is 2 mg nocte.

questions.question_text: His psychotic symptoms are under control. His mother wants to know duration of antipsychotic treatment (in months) in his case. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Recommended duration of antipsychotic treatment after first episode is 15 months.

questions.question_text: After 18 months of treatment, the patient has decided to stop the medication. His mother wants to know the risk of relapse in percentage. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Risk of relapse after stopping antipsychotics is about 75%.

questions.question_text: A core trainee knows that he has to be an honest doctor and knows how to apply honesty in balance with other considerations in situations when medical errors occur causing suffering to his patients. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Phronesis is practical wisdom in applying ethical principles to real-world situations.

questions.question_text: In a multicultural society, different ethnic groups of people are supposed to have different ethical standards for evaluating acts as right or wrong. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Ethical relativism holds that moral standards vary across cultures and individuals.

questions.question_text: A lay person in the animal ethics research committee says, ‘We can judge the heart of a principal investigator by his treatment of animals’. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Categorical imperatives are universal moral laws by which actions can be judged.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old university student is referred to you for mild anxiety before an examination. She has good functioning in other areas and is involved in a wide range of university activities. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: GAF 81–90 indicates minimal symptoms and good functioning across most areas.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is referred to you for frequent shoplifting. She cannot control the impulse to steal and fulfill the diagnostic criteria for kleptomania. She was arrested earlier that resulted in serious impairment in social and occupational functioning. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: GAF 41–50 indicates serious symptoms and impairment in social/occupational functioning.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man suffers from schizophrenia and stays in a secure setting because of recurrent episodes of violence. He is unkempt with persistent inability to maintain personal hygiene. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: GAF 1–10 indicates persistent danger to self/others and inability to maintain hygiene.

questions.question_text: Her current performance IQ (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Raven’s Progressive Matrices is a nonverbal test of performance IQ.

questions.question_text: Her concrete thinking (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Goldstein’s Object Sorting Test assesses categorization and concrete thinking.

questions.question_text: Her executive function (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Wisconsin Card Sorting Test measures set-shifting and executive function.

questions.question_text: Secondary elaboration of acceptable images in a narrative manner and those images are often linked to day residue or events prior to sleep. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Manifest content is the dream as recalled, elaborated in narrative form, often reflecting day residue.

questions.question_text: The process where impulses are transferred to acceptable images. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Condensation refers to merging impulses and ideas into acceptable dream images.

questions.question_text: True meaning of the dream in expressing unconscious thoughts and wishes. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Latent content is the hidden, unconscious meaning expressed by the dream.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man with a history of epilepsy complains of sudden contractions of muscles on both sides of his body while falling asleep. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Myoclonic jerks are sudden muscle contractions occurring at sleep onset.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman complains that she sleeps at 3 am but wakes up at 10 am. She has always been late for work, and she has been dismissed by three companies. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Circadian rhythm sleep disorder involves a misaligned sleep–wake schedule.

questions.question_text: You are working in the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service. An anxious mother has brought her 10-year-old son to see you. He has body-rocking and head-banging movements at bedtime and naptimes. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Rhythmic movement disorder features stereotyped movements like rocking and head-banging at sleep onset.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man complains that it is impossible for him to sleep at normal times and his sleep-wake cycle is changing every day after he developed bilateral blindness as a result of cataracts. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Non-24-hour sleep-wake syndrome occurs in blind individuals who lack light perception and have a free-running circadian rhythm.

questions.question_text: Edward Oxford, who attempted to murder Queen Victoria, was 18 years old when the offence occurred in 1840. He described in his notebooks how he was to be the instrument of a plot of an imaginary secret society, and to this end, had purchased pistols and practiced with them. Because of the medical evidence of mental illness, the defence succeeded and a verdict of ‘guilty but insane’ was issued. After the trial, Oxford was admitted to Bethlem Royal Hospital. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: The Edward Oxford trial established the irresistible impulse test in British law.

questions.question_text: Earl Ferrers lived with his wife at Stanton Harold in Leicestershire in the mid-1700s. He was an alcoholic, and his chronic drinking led to psychosis and rage. He also made a false accusation against a man, Mr Johnson, who lived in his estate for robbery. He ordered Mr Johnson to come to his house and then shot him. Later, Mr Johnson died and Earl Ferrers was charged with murder. He was tried by his fellows in the Tower of London. A plea of insanity was refused and Earl Ferrers was found guilty and sentenced to hang. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Earl Ferrers’ trial in 1760 was the first recorded use of psychiatric testimony in an English court.

questions.question_text: James Hadfield fired a pistol at King George III at the Theatre Royal during the playing of the national anthem on the evening of 15 May 1800. Hadfield was tried for treason and was defended by a prominent barrister. Later, Hadfield pleaded insanity. Three doctors testified that Hadfield had delusions which were the consequence of his earlier head injuries. Hadfield was detained in Bethlem Royal Hospital for the rest of his life. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Hadfield’s case introduced the concept of the ‘offspring of a delusion’ in the insanity defence.

questions.question_text: Children see the world from their own standpoint but cannot appreciate that other people may see things differently. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Egocentrism is characteristic of the preoperational stage (ages 2–7 years).

questions.question_text: An infant can add new information into the existing schema. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Assimilation and circular reactions occur in the sensorimotor stage (0–2 years) as infants incorporate new experiences into existing schemas.

questions.question_text: An adolescent can hold several possible explanations in mind for a phenomenon and think of possible outcomes. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Hypothetico-deductive thinking emerges in the formal operational stage (adolescence onward), allowing consideration of multiple hypotheses.
